sections.title: The Divine Spark in the Idolatrous Religions
sections.html:
Maran Ha-Rav Kook wrote that when we come to discuss the various religions, we must know that the world is conducted by God's providence so as to raise human beings gradually toward their blissful purpose. "Therefore we know that as long as avoda zara (idolatry) is still found in the world, it has a purpose." For as long as people's thinking is crude, they cannot receive guidance from an abstract faith in the One God, and they need a tangible faith in idols, which gives them basic rules of derekh eretz (proper conduct) and morality. For in every religion there is a divine spark of morality that animates it, by force of which it establishes rules of good and evil. On this basis humanity can advance gradually toward faith in God's unity and its moral guidance (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor, chapters 8; 14:1).

That is to say, even according to the idolatrous outlook, above the idols that express all the forces revealed in the world there are values of truth and goodness. Thus we find in all the stories of the ancient gods (the myths) that although the power of the gods is great, it is limited, and they too are subject to the decree of fate. Moreover, their own deeds also affect their fate, and any idol that crosses a certain limit, and sins through excessive lust or excessive pride, or through extreme disregard for other gods, will be punished by higher and stronger forces. These higher forces express a higher order of values, and within them is hidden belief in God, the source of life and goodness. As it is stated (Malakhi 1:11): "For from the rising of the sun to its setting My name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to My name, and a pure offering; for My name is great among the nations, says the Lord of Hosts." The Sages explained (Menaḥot 110a) that all idol worshippers call God "Elaha de-Elahaya", "the God of gods".

The meaning of this is that even when human understanding was crude, and there was hardly anyone in the world who did not believe that the idols ruled the various forces and that it was worthwhile to bow down to them in order to receive help from them, in the depths of people's hearts there was belief in a "supreme God", the source of truth and morality. However, the vast majority of human beings found no meaning in this, and only a few rose to direct their prayer also to the God of gods, and they were considered worshippers of avoda zara be-shituf (idolatry in association with God). Among them were exceptional individuals who delved into the source of their faith, directed the main part of their prayer to the God of gods, improved their ways with great devotion, and, within the darkness of the idolatrous religions, strove greatly to strengthen the values of truth and goodness in people's hearts. The finest of them even merited ru'aḥ ha-kodesh (divine inspiration), as Tanna De-vei Eliyahu says (chapter 9): "I call heaven and earth to witness that whether man or woman, whether manservant or maidservant, whether gentile or Jew, all according to one's deeds, ru'aḥ ha-kodesh rests upon him." With the help of the ru'aḥ ha-kodesh that rested upon them, they deepened their faith in the source of life, and although they did not abolish idol worship, they established good and beneficial laws and customs within the idolatrous frameworks. Of them Rabbi Meir said: "Even a gentile who engages in Torah is like a High Priest," as it is stated (Vayikra 18:5): "You shall keep My statutes and My ordinances, which a man shall do and live by them": "it does not say 'Kohanim, Levites and Israelites', but 'a man'." The Gemara explained that their Torah concerns the seven Noahide commandments, which contain the foundations of faith and morality (Sanhedrin 59a). Rav Kook added that it is possible that the leaders of the religions even received help from Heaven to perform wonders, so that their listeners would accept the religion that would advance their moral state.1

sections.title: The Founding of Religions
sections.html:
As a further explanation of Rav Kook's words, one can say that from the fact that Benei Noaḥ (non-Jews) are commanded to keep the seven commandments, it follows that every people must found a religion for itself, for it is impossible to keep the seven commandments without there being a religion based on a higher power from which the commandments will draw their validity and worth. In addition, in order to fulfil the seven commandments it is necessary to define what each prohibition includes, and the various religions help to define these prohibitions and give them validity. For example, in order to fulfil the prohibition of robbery, one must first establish the laws of acquisition, by which it is determined in what manner an object or land becomes a person's property, and consequently it is forbidden to rob him of it. Likewise with the commandment concerning forbidden sexual relations: only after defining when a marriage takes effect can one determine when a woman is considered married, and consequently the prohibition of "a married woman" applies to her. Likewise, in order to fulfil the commandment of dinim (establishing courts of law), it is necessary to establish laws for maintaining public order, what the punishment of one who transgresses them is, and who the judges authorised to judge will be.

As we have learned (5:8-10), according to most poskim (halakhic authorities) there is no prohibition for Benei Noaḥ to practise avoda zara be-shituf. It follows that as long as the founders of religions believed that God is the God of gods, even if they believed that beneath Him there are various idols with independent power and therefore bowed down to them, they did not transgress a prohibition. And if they needed this in order to establish belief in the God of gods and to strengthen the members of their people in keeping the seven commandments, then, according to their situation, they even acted properly. The terrible sins occurred when they stopped associating belief in God, did not keep the rules of morality, and in the name of their idolatrous faith went on doing wickedness and sin.2

sections.title: The Attitude toward the Various Religions
sections.html:
Maran Ha-Rav Kook explained at length the importance of understanding the good and beneficial aspects of the various religions, and the damage caused by viewing them in a solely negative light. As he wrote: "The narrow-mindedness that causes one to see in everything outside the bounds of the particular nation… only ugliness and impurity is one of the terrible darknesses that cause the general destruction of the whole edifice of spiritual good, whose light every refined soul awaits." For "love of all creatures must be alive in the heart and soul: love of every human being in particular, and love of all the nations." And all the expressions of hatred toward the gentiles are "only against the wickedness and filth in the world." This love must exist "despite all the differences of opinions, religions and faiths, and despite all the distinctions of races and climates. It is right to penetrate to the depths of the minds of the various nations and groups, to learn as much as possible their character and their traits, in order to know how to ground human love on foundations that approach practice." He further wrote that "without inner love, from the depths of heart and soul, to do good to all the nations," it is impossible to fulfil the special destiny of Israel, to bring the word of God and His blessing to the world. And there is no need to fear that the positive attitude toward the nations of the world and their religions will impair loyalty to Israel, for only out of love of all creatures can love of the nation reach its highest level (Middot Ha-re'iya, Ahava 5; 10).

The Torah did indeed forbid us any tolerance toward avoda zara, so that we can fulfil our special role: to reveal in the world the light of faith in God's unity and to perfect the world under the kingship of the Almighty. Therefore we are commanded to distance ourselves with self-sacrifice from any trace of avoda zara. In addition, so that Jews are not drawn after avoda zara, it is a mitzva to express the shame of avoda zara and the disgrace of its worshippers, "to the degree that is fitting to arouse in our souls the greatness of the good and the holy inheritance that has fallen to our lot, that He separated us from those who go astray and gave us the Torah of truth and planted eternal life within us; that we need not occupy ourselves with such lowly forms of guidance, and relative to us they are astray." Yet together with this one must know that, according to the level of the gentiles' souls, it is possible that by being loyal to their idolatrous religion they are "behaving as befits them" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 14:1). For in each of the religions there is a spark of the divine light, which finds expression "in various systems of education for human culture, for the rectification of its spirit and matter, its moment and its world, its individual and its community, but they are at different levels. Just as the power of growth is one, and is revealed in the cedar in Lebanon and in the hyssop on the wall, but in the first it comes in a rich and abundant form and in the second in a poor and meagre form, so too the light of the divine spark comes in the highest of the religions and faiths in a rich manner and an exalted way, and in the lowest of them in a blurred manner, in poverty and lowliness" (Orot, Zer'onim 6).

Accordingly, even regarding the lowest idolatrous religion, "one should not decide about the entire religion that it is an error," for perhaps it was suited to them in the past in order to raise them somewhat. And there are levels among the religions, and some are more refined "in morality, in character traits and derekh eretz, and consequently their customs and ways of avoda zara are not as abominable and full of loathsomeness as others" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 14:1). And sometimes one religion is more refined in a certain area and less so in other areas. Generally there is a correspondence between the degree of idolatrous corporealisation and the moral level; but sometimes, despite the crude corporealisation, the leaders of that religion rose to establish more moral ordinances; and likewise the reverse: sometimes the leaders of a lofty religion turned it to evil, to terrible acts of wickedness.3

sections.title: It Is Fitting for a Person to Continue in His Religion
sections.html:
Seemingly, because of the severity of the prohibition of avoda zara, it would be fitting to say that every gentile is obligated to leave his idolatrous religion immediately. In practice, however, Maran Ha-Rav Kook wrote that this is not correct. For even the exceptional individuals among the nations of the world, who knew that God is the God of gods, the source of all forces, did not abolish idol worship. This is because they knew that faith in the One God is too abstract and lofty, and that without the faith resting on tangible forces called idols, and being strengthened through worship directed toward them, they would not succeed in establishing the moral values that would elevate the members of their people and religion.

Thus, for example, many people who set up statues of wood and stone in their homes out of belief that they would help them, when their evil inclination overcame them and they wanted to murder, commit adultery or steal, restrained themselves from doing evil because they imagined that the statue was looking at them with angry eyes and was about to punish them. Thus, with the help of the idolatrous rites performed in temples and homes, many people were deterred to a certain extent from doing evil. And if we were to demand of them "to accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven and abandon their idols before they were prepared for it… then, instead of doing them good as we imagine, we would do them harm. For they would not be able to absorb the divine light," and the crude fear of avoda zara that kept them from grave sins we would abolish. By contrast, if they continue to keep the laws of their religion, they will rise gradually until they merit reaching the true level of faith that is drawn through the light of Israel. Therefore, relative to their level, their religion has "religious worth". And from afar we can recognise and respect them for drawing near to the light of God in their own way, "and think that they are acting as befits them in holding on to the heritage of their fathers and to the customs that the elders of their nation instituted for them" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 14:1).

Rav Kook explained that this is the deep reason why it is forbidden to teach Torah to a gentile, to the point that the Sages said (Sanhedrin 59a): "A gentile who engages in Torah is liable to death, as it is stated (Devarim 33:4): 'Moshe commanded us a Torah, an inheritance [of the congregation of Yaakov]': it is an inheritance for us, and not for them." For there is a concern that the lofty teachings will harm one who has not yet been prepared for them.4

That is to say, the aim is that every religion should rise gradually in the direction of a more abstract and more moral faith. And this happens because even within "the darkness of avoda zara, there can be found pure-hearted individuals who will wish to rebuke and improve the ways of their people; and because they recognise that the true, pure divine light is greater than their power, they will guide it [i.e. their people], according to its worth, with good codes of conduct and customs that bring it to a better perfection in the future" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 14:1). Until, over time, they will find ways to interpret their religion in a deeper and more abstract manner, will remove the dross of crude corporealisation, and will raise souls to higher faith and morality (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 46).5

sections.title: Christianity and Islam
sections.html:
Maran Ha-Rav Kook wrote that above the idolatrous religions stand Christianity and Islam, which were influenced by the Tanakh and by Israel, and they are closer to the light of God. It is also reasonable that some of the leaders and sages of Christianity and Islam merited help from Heaven, by virtue of their striving to elevate people, tribes and nations as befitted them. And it is even possible that Heaven helped them perform tangible wonders, in order to strengthen their words in the eyes of their listeners, so that they would thereby advance in faith and morality (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 8; 46).

However, there is a great deficiency in these religions: they do not recognise the central role of Israel in revealing the word of God and His blessing to the world, and instead they presume to replace them, while harming Jews and Judaism. From this stems a further deficiency: these religions lack guidance toward constant self-perfection that can elevate humanity without end, and consequently they cannot create a centre around which all human beings will unite. Therefore it is necessary that over time the Christians and the Muslims will be cleansed of hatred of Israel, and will be able to draw from the source of the faith of Israel illumination and guidance, as is fitting and suitable for them, for the sake of constant elevation and tikkun olam (rectification of the world) (based on Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 8).6

But even now, when many of them hate Israel and have not yet purified their faith of every trace of idolatry, together with criticism of the evil deeds that stem from this, it is fitting to respect the foundations of faith and morality in their religion, by which they have succeeded in raising many people to good character traits and to the love and fear of God. Therefore the members of these religions are commanded "to walk in the ways of their lawgivers, who are held in their nation to be holy men according to their worth and character" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 14:1). Likewise, "it is fitting for every person of complete understanding to comprehend that those who engage in them according to the tradition in their hands are engaging in the service of God according to their worth" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 8).

In addition, one should see in them the advance of a further stage in the process of refining faith and morality, from crude idol worship toward pure faith in God (Kuzari 4:23; Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 11:4; Ramban, above 6:7).

sections.title: Conversion from One's Religion
sections.html:
Maran Ha-Rav Kook wrote that it is not fitting for a person to change his religion, for every religion also expresses the social and national character through which it took shape, and one who abandons it betrays his family, his people and their good values. And if the religion to which he is converting is inferior in terms of faith and morality to his previous religion, he also "goes backward and darkens the light of his soul, apart from completely perverting the paths of his morality by betraying his nation, which nurtured him and raised him; and he deserves to be called a scoundrel, and will not go unpunished" (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 8).

However, if he converts from an idolatrous religion to Christianity or Islam, his sin is open to discussion, for although he harms his people for the moment, it is possible that benefit for humanity and for his people will grow from this, since he is moving to a religion that is closer to the perfection of man, "because the recognition of the unity of God, blessed be He, will in any case bring blessing to the whole world." However, "the matter is not properly clarified," because Christianity and Islam too "cannot bring the success of man to its purpose," for they cannot gather around themselves all the shades and virtues in all the religions and nations; and so it is possible that it is preferable that he not betray his religion, but rather rise within it to higher levels of faith and morality.

An example can be brought from the Hindu religion: although there is idolatry in it, since it has a central stream that emphasises the one source and educates toward deep morality, leaving it in favour of Christianity or Islam may be considered a descent, as happened to many of those who converted to Islam, who harmed themselves and their people more than they benefited them.

Since every change of religion involves a betrayal of the good tradition that a person received from his family and his people, conversion to Judaism too is complex; and therefore the Sages said, "Converts are as difficult for Israel as a sapaḥat (a skin affliction)" (Yevamot 47b; see Peninei Halakha, Giyur 1:10-11). However, since the faith of Israel brings blessing to all the nations, and the convert wishes to join Israel in order to add strength to them for the good of all humanity, there is no betrayal in this. Moreover, over time he or his descendants, by virtue of their origin, will be able to understand better the soul of the nation from which they came, and from the source of Israel they will be able to bestow upon it knowledge, morality and blessing, as suits it (Li-nvukhei Ha-dor 8; 52).

sections.title: The Vision of Faith and the Future of the Religions
sections.html:
The general movement of humanity is in a positive direction: from low and crude understandings to lofty and abstract understandings; from a moral outlook aimed at survival to an idealistic aspiration to add goodness and blessing to society, to the nation and to humanity; from idolatrous faith to faith in the One God. This process is made up of countless choices by people, which led to achievements and failures. The process involves suffering and wars, and takes place within national and religious frameworks. The more people choose to seek truth and goodness, the more they advance, and with less suffering, each person and each people according to the quality of their choice. At the centre of the process of ascent toward tikkun olam stands the Jewish people, which was chosen by God to reveal His light and blessing to the world. In proportion to the greatness of its mission, so is its path long and its sufferings many, its trials and the obstacles before it great, and great are its consolations and great its salvation, through which the world is progressively redeemed; until faith in the One God becomes the heritage of all humanity, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 2:17-18): "And the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day. And the idols shall utterly pass away." And it is stated (Zekharia 14:9): "And the Lord shall be King over all the earth; on that day the Lord shall be One and His name One." And for this we pray: "to remove the abominations from the earth, and the idols will be utterly cut off, to perfect the world under the kingship of the Almighty" (the Aleinu Le-shabe'aḥ prayer).

However, this is not an aspiration that all the nations and religions should cease to exist, for every religion has a special hue that expresses the character of the people in which it was created. Therefore the vision is that every religion will be cleansed of all its flaws and will reveal its own special way in the service of God and in adding blessing to the world. As it is stated (Zekharia 9:7): "And I will remove his blood from his mouth, and his abominations from between his teeth, and he too shall remain for our God." "And I will remove his blood from his mouth": murderousness, robbery and the other moral flaws between man and his fellow; "and his abominations from between his teeth": the dross of idolatry; and then "he too shall remain for our God": to add blessing to the world. As it is stated (Tzefania 3:9): "For then I will turn to the peoples a clear language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, to serve Him with one consent."

Together with each people's special attachment to its religion, all humanity will be united through the connection of all the nations to the people of Israel and to its holy centre in Jerusalem, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 56:7): "And I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon My altar, for My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples." And it is stated: "And it shall come to pass in the end of days that the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established at the top of the mountains and shall be exalted above the hills, and all the nations shall flow to it. And many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Yaakov, and He will teach us of His ways and we will walk in His paths; for out of Zion shall go forth Torah, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And He shall judge between the nations and shall rebuke many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more" (Yeshayahu 2:2-4). And it is stated: "And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid… They shall not hurt nor destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea" (ibid. 11:6-9).7
